questions.prompt: What are the three steps in the SwiftUI layout process?

options.text: Parent proposes size, child chooses size, and parent places child.
options.explanation: Right. Parent proposes a size, child picks its size, and parent places it.

options.text: Parent forces child size, GPU draws images, and Core Animation scales.
options.explanation: Parents propose space in SwiftUI; they cannot force a size on a child.

options.text: Child claims the full screen, parent resizes the window, and views cache.
options.explanation: Layout starts when the parent proposes available space down to the child.

options.text: UIKit builds constraints, SwiftUI runs a solver, and views update.
options.explanation: SwiftUI uses its own three-step layout pass, not UIKit constraints.

questions.prompt: How does a Spacer behave when placed inside an HStack?

options.text: It stretches vertically to fill all available screen height.
options.explanation: Spacers expand along the main direction of their stack, which is horizontal here.

options.text: It expands horizontally to push nearby views apart.
options.explanation: Right. In an HStack, the main direction is horizontal, so Spacer expands sideways.

options.text: It stays fixed at twenty points on all iPhone and iPad screens.
options.explanation: Spacer is flexible and expands to fill empty space; it is not fixed.

options.text: It shrinks to zero points unless you add a frame width.
options.explanation: Spacer expands to fill empty space without needing an explicit width.

questions.prompt: In what order does a ZStack layer its child views on screen?

options.text: Randomly, depending on which child view draws fastest on GPU.
options.explanation: Drawing order always follows the exact order you write in code.

options.text: Front to back, where the first view written sits on the top.
options.explanation: The first view written sits at the back, not on top.

options.text: Back to front, where earlier views sit behind later views.
options.explanation: Right. Views written first sit in the back, and later views layer on top.

options.text: Alphabetically, sorted by the name of each child view struct.
options.explanation: ZStack uses your code order, not alphabetical order.

questions.prompt: What happens when child content is larger than its .frame() size?

options.text: The app crashes right away with a fatal layout error.
options.explanation: Overflowing a frame does not crash a SwiftUI app.

options.text: SwiftUI shrinks the child text until it fits inside the frame.
options.explanation: Text does not shrink unless you add extra scaling modifiers.

options.text: The frame grows larger to match the overflowing child view.
options.explanation: A fixed frame keeps its size and does not expand for larger content.

options.text: The content spills outside the frame unless .clipped() is added.
options.explanation: Right. Frames do not clip overflowing views by default.

questions.prompt: What does a VStack do when you omit the spacing parameter?

options.text: It uses an adaptive platform default gap between child views.
options.explanation: Right. SwiftUI applies standard system spacing when spacing is nil.

options.text: It sets the gap between all stacked children to zero points.
options.explanation: Setting the gap to zero requires writing spacing: 0.

options.text: It stretches each child view to touch the edges of the screen.
options.explanation: VStack does not stretch child frames to the screen edges.

options.text: It fails to compile because spacing is a required parameter.
options.explanation: Spacing is optional and defaults to nil.

questions.prompt: How can you make a view stretch to fill the full width its parent offers?

options.text: By adding the .fillParentWidth() modifier to the view struct.
options.explanation: SwiftUI has no modifier named fillParentWidth.

options.text: By applying .frame(maxWidth: .infinity) to the view.
options.explanation: Right. Setting maxWidth to infinity lets the frame accept all offered width.

options.text: By wrapping the view inside a custom UIKit layout class.
options.explanation: Native SwiftUI uses .frame(maxWidth: .infinity) for full-width views.

options.text: By setting the view layout priority value to minus ninety-nine.
options.explanation: Negative layout priority gives a view lower priority; it does not stretch it.

questions.prompt: How does SwiftUI share limited horizontal space among views in an HStack?

options.text: It cuts off all views equally no matter how flexible they are.
options.explanation: SwiftUI does not cut views equally; it respects how flexible each view is.

options.text: It gives space randomly to whichever view was written first.
options.explanation: Space sharing follows clear rules based on view flexibility and priority.

options.text: It offers space to least flexible views first, then shares the rest.
options.explanation: Right. Rigid views take what they need first, then flexible views share the rest.

options.text: It wraps overflowing views onto a second row below the first.
options.explanation: HStack never wraps views to a new row. Use a grid when wrapping is needed.

questions.prompt: What does the .layoutPriority(_:) modifier do in SwiftUI?

options.text: It sets the thread priority for background data loading tasks.
options.explanation: Layout priority controls view sizing, not background thread speed.

options.text: It forces views to draw at sixty frames per second during scroll.
options.explanation: Layout priority does not control display refresh rates.

options.text: It changes the drawing order of views inside a ZStack.
options.explanation: ZStack order comes from code order, not layout priority.

options.text: It lets higher-priority views claim available space first.
options.explanation: Right. Views with higher layout priority receive space offers before siblings.

questions.prompt: Which alignment lines up text views along the bottom of their first text line in an HStack?

options.text: .firstTextBaseline, which aligns views by their first text baseline.
options.explanation: Right. .firstTextBaseline lines up text views along their first line baseline.

options.text: .centerLeading, which forces text to line up with the left edge.
options.explanation: centerLeading is not a valid alignment for HStack.

options.text: .topLeading, which lines up views at the upper left corner.
options.explanation: HStack uses vertical alignment values, not two-axis Alignment values.

options.text: .stretchToFill, which stretches text letters to fill stack height.
options.explanation: SwiftUI has no stretchToFill alignment and does not stretch letters.

questions.prompt: Why can an empty Spacer stretch a small card wider than expected?

options.text: Because Spacers automatically draw full-width background images.
options.explanation: Spacers are invisible views and do not draw images.

options.text: Because Spacers expand greedily to fill all remaining stack space.
options.explanation: Right. Spacers take all leftover space, stretching the container.

options.text: Because Spacers remove clip shapes from their parent containers.
options.explanation: Spacers do not remove clip shapes on parent views.

options.text: Because Spacers crash when placed inside custom view structs.
options.explanation: Spacers run safely anywhere in a stack, but they expand greedily.

questions.prompt: What does a Divider view draw when placed inside a VStack?

options.text: A vertical line that stretches from the top edge to the bottom edge.
options.explanation: Inside a VStack, Divider draws a horizontal line across the width.

options.text: A clickable link line that pushes a new screen onto the stack.
options.explanation: Divider is a visual line only. It does not handle navigation.

options.text: A thin horizontal separating line across the width of the stack.
options.explanation: Right. In a vertical stack, Divider spans horizontally between rows.

options.text: An invisible spacer that doubles the height of nearby views.
options.explanation: Divider draws a visible line, not an invisible spacer.

questions.prompt: Why does SwiftUI layout avoid constraint conflicts and layout loops?

options.text: Because SwiftUI views compute sizes on background CPU threads.
options.explanation: SwiftUI layout runs on the main thread, not background threads.

options.text: Because all SwiftUI views are forced to a fixed 320-point width.
options.explanation: SwiftUI supports dynamic widths on every iPhone and iPad screen.

options.text: Because it solves systems of math equations in multiple passes.
options.explanation: UIKit Auto Layout uses a constraint solver; SwiftUI uses one pass.

options.text: Because layout runs in one pass: proposals down and sizes up.
options.explanation: Right. Proposals flow down and chosen sizes flow up in a single pass.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between frame alignment and stack alignment?

options.text: Frame alignment sets Z-axis depth, and stack alignment sets X-axis.
options.explanation: Frame alignment places a view inside its frame box, not Z-depth.

options.text: Frame aligns a view in its box; stack aligns siblings together.
options.explanation: Right. Frame aligns one child in its box; stack aligns siblings with each other.

options.text: Stack alignment works only on iPad, while frame alignment is iPhone.
options.explanation: Both alignments work the same way on iPhone and iPad.

options.text: Frame alignment needs UIKit Auto Layout constraints to run.
options.explanation: SwiftUI frame alignment is native and does not use UIKit constraints.

questions.prompt: How does SwiftUI treat views with different layout priorities in an HStack?

options.text: It hides every view with priority 0 if any sibling has priority 1.

options.text: It offers space to higher-priority views before lower ones.
options.explanation: Right. Higher-priority views get first claim on available space.

options.text: It ignores layout priority unless views sit inside a List.

questions.prompt: Explain the three steps of the SwiftUI layout process. Write 2 to 5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains Step 1: the parent view proposes an available size to the child view.
Explains Step 2: the child view chooses its own final size and reports it back.
Explains Step 3: the parent places the child inside its space.

questions.modelAnswer: SwiftUI layout happens in three steps. First, the parent view proposes an available size to its child view. Second, the child chooses its own final size from its content and tells the parent. Third, the parent places the child inside its space. The parent cannot force a size on the child.

questions.prompt: Compare how Spacer behaves inside an HStack versus inside a VStack. Write 2 to 5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that a Spacer expands along the main direction of its stack.
States that in an HStack, the Spacer expands horizontally to push views left and right.
States that in a VStack, the Spacer expands vertically to push views top and bottom.

questions.modelAnswer: A Spacer is a flexible view that fills empty space along the main direction of its stack. Inside an HStack, the main direction is horizontal, so Spacer expands sideways to push views left and right. Inside a VStack, the main direction is vertical, so Spacer expands up and down to push views apart.

questions.prompt: Explain what happens when content is larger than a .frame() size, and describe how to clip it. Write 2 to 5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that .frame() sets a proposed size and layout box but does not clip content by default.
States that overflowing text or shapes spill visually outside the frame edges.
Identifies .clipped() as the modifier that cuts off overflowing content.

questions.modelAnswer: Calling .frame(width:height:) creates a layout box with a proposed size, but it does not clip content by default. If child text or shapes are larger than the frame, they spill visually outside the edges. Nearby views still line up against the frame box, which can cause overlaps. To cut off overflowing content, chain .clipped() after .frame(...).

questions.prompt: How does SwiftUI share space among child views in an HStack when width is limited, and how can you give one view priority? Write 2 to 5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that SwiftUI offers space to the least flexible views first.
States that remaining space is divided among flexible views.
Identifies .layoutPriority(_:) as the modifier that lets a view claim space first.

questions.modelAnswer: When horizontal space is tight in an HStack, SwiftUI does not split space equally. First, it offers space to the least flexible views so they get what they need. Then it shares any leftover space among flexible views like Spacer or wrapping text. To give one view first claim on space, apply a higher .layoutPriority(_:) value than the default 0.

questions.prompt: Explain how ZStack layers views and how its drawing order affects user taps. Write 2 to 5 sentences.

rubric.criterion: Explains that ZStack draws views in code order from back to front.
States that views written earlier sit behind views written later.
Explains that a solid view written last sits on top and can block taps to views behind it.

questions.modelAnswer: ZStack layers child views from back to front in the order you write them in code. Views written earlier sit in the back, and views written later sit on top. This order also controls which view receives user taps. If you put a solid color after a button, the color covers the button and blocks taps, so always place backgrounds first.
